messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amir is a 41-year-old fast food worker who lives alone in a small one-bedroom apartment in a suburban strip mall complex. Two years ago, while working the closing shift at a different restaurant, he witnessed a customer pull a knife on his coworker during a dispute over an order. The altercation ended when a security guard tackled the man, but not before Amir saw the blade glint under the fluorescent lights and heard the coworker scream. He has not worked the closing shift at a new job since, but the memory itself is not what troubles him—it is the ordinary moments that suddenly feel dangerous.

The same time of day the incident occurred, around 10:45 p.m., Amir’s body tenses without his permission. When he is standing at the fry station and the digital clock hits that hour, his hands start to tremble. He learned to request earlier shifts, but the schedule occasionally rotates, and on those nights he becomes hypervigilant, scanning the dining area for any sign of conflict. He has come to believe that something terrible is always about to happen when the evening drags past that threshold. This sense of impending threat carries over to other triggers. Being criticised or corrected by his manager, even gently, sets off a cascade of alarm. A simple, “Can you wrap that burger a little tighter?” makes Amir feel as though he is being singled out, that the criticism is a prelude to escalation. He now avoids eye contact with his supervisors and braces himself before each shift, certain that any correction could spiral into confrontation.

Loud noises—the slam of a metal tray, the hiss of the steam cleaner, a dropped plate—make him flinch and search for exits. These sounds, he is convinced, signal immediate danger. The threat does not dissipate quickly; his heart races, his breathing quickens, and he feels a pressing need to retreat to the back storage room, which he has designated as the only place he can calm down. He only feels safe in that narrow, windowless space, where the lighting is dim and nobody can surprise him. Outside of work, his apartment has become a fortress. He rarely leaves except for his shifts, and even then he hurries home directly.

Delays of any kind now feel catastrophic. When a customer order takes too long, or when his bus is late, Amir’s mind immediately jumps to the worst scenario. A staggered delivery of supplies means someone is trying to cause trouble. A longer-than-usual shift means management is plotting against him. He cannot tolerate waiting, because waiting feels like the moment before violence. This hypervigilance has cost him friendships and made dating nearly impossible. He turned down invitations from coworkers because the thought of being outside his safe zone—his apartment or the storage room—is too overwhelming.

Amir finally sought help after a particularly bad night. His schedule had been pushed to the evening again, and a loud argument between customers at the counter triggered a full-blown panic. He hid in the storage room for nearly half an hour, trembling, convinced that the argument would turn physical and that he would be drawn in. His manager found him and threatened to fire him if he could not manage his “nerves.” That ultimatum, combined with his own exhaustion, pushed Amir to call a clinic the next morning. What he fears most is that he cannot keep working, but he does not know how to stop the cycle—each criticism, each loud noise, each clock hand reaching ten forty-five renews the feeling that he is no longer safe anywhere.
